FUN FACT: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade began as a Christmas parade on that same day, organized by the Jewish Straus Family, who owned Macy's. 

In 1924, back before Judeo-Christianity had spread like cancer, this was highly offensive to Christians who, at the time, accused them of commercializing Christ's birth for extra shekels. They claimed that it was an attempt to sully a Christian holiday with vulgar commercialization. 

The Allied Patriotic Societies tried to stop the Jewish businessmen from pimping the faith to sell extra goods. They accused the Jewish elite of trying to lure Christians away from the Thanksgiving worship services that traditionally took place in the morning, and also accused them of "villifying the pilgrims."

Christian groups asked the New York City government and police not to allow the parade to interfere with Christian worship on this holy day. They refused and instead gave them a police escort. 

At the end of the parade, Santa was crowned "King of the Kiddies." 

The Jews had finally given someone a crown that wasn't made of thorns. And it was given to Santa. 

A few years later, it became the "Thanksgiving Day Parade" and the time was begrudgingly moved to the afternoon to "accommodate" the Christians who worshipped in the morning. Soon, Christian services on that day disappeared because churches could not compete with the merchants and banking class. 

Straus, by the way, was one of the wealthy Jews who crafted and propagandized the "Blackstone Memorial," pretending to be an evangelical petition, calling for a Jewish ethnostate in Palestine. 

Straus famously gave 150k (a huge sum back then) to Rabbi Stephen Wise to expand his voice, teaching that Jews should embrace Jesus' identity as a "Jewish" teacher in order to soften the majority Christian culture toward Jews. He was subsequently condemned by the Union of Orthodox Rabbis for trying to claim Jesus as Jewish.

Historians point to the parades by Macy's and Gimble's as milestones in Christmas's commercialization. It put vain consumerism on a literal parade, and expanded the "shopping season" by a full month. 

Thanksgiving is one of the purest, most holy days of Christian tradition. It's designed to give thanks to God. That's it. It's that simple. And beautiful. 

But now, when your pastor complains that Christmas SOMEHOW became overly commercialized, understand who came along, looked at that pure expression of Christian faith, and thought, "We can make money off of this." 

We have Good Friday. Their religion has Black Friday. We are not the same. 

So, enjoy your day. Feast in Christ's honor. Celebrate God's blessings. 

And pray as a family that God might restore our uniquely CHRISTIAN nation, without a hyphen and a "Judeo" in front of it.

🔻 Iran says silence of disarmament bodies over US-Israeli aggression undermines their credibility

📌 London, IRNA – Iran’s Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the United Nations and other international organizations in Austria, Reza Najafi, has criticized international disarmament and non-proliferation bodies for their silence over the US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran, stressing that their inaction has seriously undermined the credibility and effectiveness of these organizations.

The Iranian envoy made the remarks on Wednesday at the 67th session of the Preparatory Commission of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO), held in Vienna from November 25 to 27.
​
The following is the full text of the Iranian envoy’s speech:
​
While welcoming you, I assure you of my delegation’s full support, and express my appreciation to Dr. Floyd for his opening remarks. I align myself with the statement of G77 and China.
​
In June 2025 and February 2026, the United States and the Israeli regime launched war of aggressions against my country under the big lie of preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. They committed war crimes and crimes against humanity, and killed thousands of our civilians, including more than 600 children, 168 of whom were brutally killed in a girls’ primary school targeted by US missiles in a triple tap strike.
​
Their aggressions including against peaceful safeguarded nuclear facilities, is an aggression against the very object and purpose of the CTBT. It can push it further away from its entry into force. Neither the Treaty members nor its Preparatory Commission can disregard such attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities, given the interrelated nature of nuclear non-proliferation, disarmament and international peace and security.
​
We have also witnessed the silence of the relevant international bodies entrusted with responsibility for non-proliferation, disarmament and international security. Such silence coupled with support for the aggressors demonstrates their growing irrelevance and raises serious questions about their credibility, particularly when they expect their member states to demonstrate unwavering commitment while failing to uphold their own obligations.
​
As we commemorate the 30th anniversary of the CTBT’s opening for signature, the treaty has yet to enter into force. We reiterate our principled position that certain Nuclear-Weapon States bear a particular responsibility to take concrete measures towards facilitating the Treaty’s entry into force.
​
The increasing rhetoric advocating the resumption of nuclear-weapon test explosions by the US President is of particular concern. Such statement constitutes a clear violation of the US commitment to avoid any action that undermines the object and purpose of the Treaty prior to its entry into force. It also undermines the established norm against nuclear testing, and increases the risk of triggering a cycle of renewed nuclear test explosions.
​
Furthermore, the activities conducted by the United States involving chemical high explosives, particularly subcritical experiments, raise serious concerns regarding their compatibility with the objectives, letter and spirit of the CTBT. Such activities undermine confidence in the integrity and credibility of the Treaty's verification regime.
​
We emphasize that the preservation of the integrity and credibility of the CTBT requires strict adherence to the maintenance of the moratorium on nuclear-weapon test explosions, and the avoidance of any conduct that could undermine its object and purpose.
​
Additionally, the CTBT should not be considered in isolation from the NPT, but rather as an integral component of the broader nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation framework. Its objectives . . .

Good morning from the Galilee!

In just a few hours, families across the United States will gather to celebrate Thanksgiving.

On October 3, 1863, three months after the Union victory at Gettysburg, President Abraham Lincoln called on Americans to set aside the last Thursday of November as a day of thanksgiving and praise to God. In 1939, President Franklin D. Roosevelt moved the holiday a week earlier to extend the Christmas shopping season. The change met with public resistance, and in 1941 Congress made the fourth Thursday of November the official date.

I believe it’s a great blessing when a nation pauses to give thanks to the Lord. But just as with Christmas, if the day becomes all about shopping, eating, and watching football, what makes it different from any other day?

Here in Israel, Yom Kippur looks like the exact opposite. Almost everything shuts down, and the big question is who made it through the day without eating! Yet we can leave God out of a fast just as easily as we can leave Him out of a feast. We wish one another an easy fast, but Scripture calls us to “afflict your souls” (Leviticus 23:27). How much attention do we give to what’s happening in our hearts?

Whether Thanksgiving is a national holiday where you live or just another Thursday, let’s remember the One to whom we give thanks. Isaiah 12:4 opens with these words:

Hodu l’Adonai - “Give thanks to the LORD.”

And Paul reminds us:

“In everything give thanks; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.”
(1 Thessalonians 5:18)

And one last thing. “Give thanks” in Hebrew is hodu. And what do we call turkey in Hebrew? Hodu! Now the Thanksgiving menu makes sense!

Happy Thanksgiving!

Awaiting His Soon Return,

Amir
